body:
What do you mean by dropping the `event.data` object? You get a completely different event, no?

Also, this is the first I've heard of this being a problem in the 20 years this API has existed so I'm rather skeptical. And that also means we can't just change this.

Greetings Anne! I hope you're doing well?

Skeptical? Just take any existing SSE script that works perfect and simply change the HTTP response: suddenly the `event.data` is force-set to `null` by browsers. I go far to distill what is actually happening and don't use frameworks or libraries; there aren't many developers who don't outright _default_ to frameworks and libraries. So if they're using off-the-shelf code they're not vested in comprehending what is going on. That's probably why you had to wait until I had a few minutes to report this ambiguity bug in the specification.

Change is not the appropriate word: clarification is. I don't work with browser vendors but it's clear that it's a simple task to remove the force-overriding of `event.data` to `null` just because the HTTP response isn't 200. Alternatively they might just presume that any error simply implies there is no data which is also incorrect. If the data is in tact it should be assigned to `event.data` no matter what.

That brings up another interesting question: should the onerror event happen because the HTTP response isn't set to 200? For all SSE instances whenever there is an error I force-close the connection and attempt to report a meaningful error message to the client. I don't mind keeping the onerror event handler being triggered by HTTP errors. However developers need the data when it's available and it's absence should imply a network connectivity issue (as what _is_ covered by the specification) whereas an HTTP error response should imply non-network connectivity issues.

Isn't the point of specifications to remove ambiguity and to ultimately help everyone involved who rely on the technology?

But there is no ambiguity here? If there's no 200 response it doesn't qualify as a SSE stream.

It seems reasonable to consider some kind of enhancement where more is exposed from the response in non-200 cases than just an error event, but that would not be a clarification.

The ambiguity is that the specification withholds if the onerror event is networking connectivity or a server error. That in turn requires pointless extra layers of work to determine if it's a network connectivity issue or a server error of which itself must be programmed to determine if the conditions to determine are successful or require further error handling. It seems this part of the specification was rushed:

`Otherwise, if res's [status](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-response-status) is not 200, or if res's `[Content-Type](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/urls-and-fetching.html#content-type)` is not `[text/event-stream](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/iana.html#text/event-stream)`, then [fail the connection](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html#fail-the-connection).`

A simple rewrite should probably look like (modified at the end):

Otherwise, if res's [status](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-response-status) is not 200, or if res's `[Content-Type](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/urls-and-fetching.html#content-type)` is not `[text/event-stream](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/iana.html#text/event-stream)`, then [fail the connection](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html#fail-the-connection) though though return the event.data object if (accessible/non-malformed(?)).

For example, if I'm importing messages from an SMTP server and 99 messages are processed just fine those responses internally would be considered 200s. If the final message is malformed in a way that the server can not compensate for and causes a problem then the connection is close with an HTTP 500 response. However this is a server error, not a networking error. So that distinction matters to the user as the server still sends what the client should access as `event.data` to return the error message. If the connection closes onerror though event.data is not set then we know it's very likely a network connectivity issue (unless the server output is malformed).

I'd consider this polish than an enhancement as an enhancement is more of a nice-to-have whereas this addresses something that is missing and important. For now, I've rewritten my platform to withhold sending the HTTP response code to the client until we've resolved the issue. Updating the specification will make a lot of people's lives easier, not just the developers though also people using software that utilizes this technology. 🙂︀

However you want to call it, you are asking for a normative change. I think filing an issue that clearly outlines the change you desire would be better. And if more people chime in that it would help them we could consider it.

Hi Anne,
I already filed the issue here and made it clear that the `event.data` object should always be made available regardless of the HTTP response from the server. I then referenced the only obvious part of the specification. Could you please clarify what you're trying to communicate that I'm missing? Once we've got it more properly formalized I'd be happy to bring it to people's attention.
